title: The watching tree (Jeremiah 1:11–12)
hookLine: an almond branch, shaked, sounds like "watching": God watches over the word
last: IT WAS NEVER ABOUT YOUR SIZE.

lines: A ROD OF AN ALMOND TREE.
cards: The next scene opens on a question, the kind a teacher asks: "Jeremiah, what seest thou?" No fire, no throne, no angels with wings. Jeremiah answers with something you could pick up on a hillside.
"I see a rod of an almond tree." A stick. A branch from a tree.
And God says: you have seen well. The vision is so ordinary that it needs the Hebrew to open it, and inside the Hebrew is a play on words, a serious one.

teach.b: Here's the play. The Hebrew word for almond is shaked.
God's answer, in the next verse, uses a word that sounds almost the same: shoked, watching, keeping watch. You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it. Shaked, shoked.
Almond, watching. In the Hebrew text the two words are written with the same letters; only the vowels differ. So the branch isn't a riddle about trees.
It's a sound that carries a promise: the word I give you is not asleep. Some readers add a picture from nature: the almond blossoms early, as if it's awake before the other trees.
That's a reader's image, not the verse's, but it fits.

In English the pun vanishes. The King James Version has "for I will hasten my word to perform it"; other translations render the word as watching, which at least points back to it. And notice what kind of vision this is.
Jeremiah has just been told he'll speak hard words to nations, yet his first lesson isn't in speaking. It's in seeing: look at a plain branch closely enough, and it turns out to be saying something.
The same question, what seest thou, comes again in the very next verse.
Jeremiah's training starts with his eyes.

how: Jews read the almond-branch vision as part of Jeremiah's opening chapter, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av; Hebrew readers hear the shaked and shoked wordplay directly.

games.q: the watching tree — tap the pairs.

s: Jeremiah's first vision is of fire and angels
it's a rod of an almond tree, a plain branch.
in Hebrew, almond and watching sound almost the same
shaked and shoked: the vision rests on the wordplay.
the King James Version keeps the pun in English
it reads "I will hasten my word"; the wordplay shows only in Hebrew.

games.q: you're Jeremiah. God asks, what seest thou? you see only a plain almond branch. what do you say?
o: I see a rod of an almond tree.
I see a vision of the end of days.
games.why: he names the plain thing, and God says he has seen well: the almond, shaked, means I am watching, shoked.

practice: Let your eyes rest on one plain thing near you, a cup, a plant, a shoe by the door, and ask Jeremiah's question quietly: what do I see? Name it plainly, then look a little longer: who made it, who uses it, what has it been through?
If nothing comes, the looking is the practice; if you pray, you can hold the verse: I watch over my word.
